635: The **urban heat island** (**UHI**) effect is a [meteorological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meteorology "Meteorology") and [climatological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climatology "Climatology") phenomenon in which [urban areas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_areas "Urban areas") experience significantly warmer temperatures than surrounding [rural areas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rural_areas "Rural areas"). The [temperature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temperature "Temperature") difference is usually larger at night than during the day,[\[1\]](#cite_note-Phelan-1) and is most apparent when [winds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wind "Wind") are weak, under [block](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Block_\(meteorology\) "Block (meteorology)") conditions, noticeably during the [summer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer "Summer") and [winter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winter "Winter"). The main cause of the UHI effect is from the modification of land surfaces, while [waste heat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waste_heat "Waste heat") generated by energy usage is a secondary contributor.[\[2\]](#cite_note-dx.doi.org-2)[\[3\]](#cite_note-3)[\[4\]](#cite_note-liyan2012-4) Urban areas occupy about 0.5% of the Earth's land surface but host more than half of the world's population.[\[5\]](#cite_note-5) As a population center grows, it tends to expand its area and increase its average temperature. Another key term is **heat island**; the term can be used to refer to any area that is relatively hotter than the surroundings, but generally refers to human-disturbed areas.[\[6\]](#cite_note-6)
636: 
637: Monthly [rainfall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Precipitation_\(meteorology\) "Precipitation (meteorology)") is greater downwind of cities, partially due to the UHI. Increases in heat within urban centers increase the length of [growing seasons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Growing_season "Growing season"), decrease [air quality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_quality "Air quality") by increasing the production of pollutants such as [ozone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozone "Ozone"), and decrease water quality as warmer waters flow into area streams and put stress on their [ecosystems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecosystem "Ecosystem").
638: 
639: Not all cities have a distinct urban heat island, and the heat island characteristics depend strongly on the background climate of the area where the [city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City "City") is located.[\[7\]](#cite_note-SUE-7) The impact in a city can significantly change based on its local environment. Heat can be reduced by [tree cover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forest_cover "Forest cover") and [green space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_green_space "Urban green space"), which act as sources of shade and promote [evaporative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evapotranspiration "Evapotranspiration") cooling.[\[8\]](#cite_note-Waldrop-8) Other options include [green roofs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_roof "Green roof"), [passive daytime radiative cooling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passive_daytime_radiative_cooling "Passive daytime radiative cooling") applications, ventilation corridors, the [use of lighter-colored surfaces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reflective_surfaces_\(climate_engineering\) "Reflective surfaces (climate engineering)"), and less absorptive building materials. These reflect more [sunlight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunlight "Sunlight") and absorb less heat.[\[9\]](#cite_note-9)[\[10\]](#cite_note-:2-10)[\[11\]](#cite_note-:13-11)
640: 
641: [Climate change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change "Climate change") is not the cause of urban heat islands, but it is causing more frequent and more intense [heat waves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_wave "Heat wave"), which in turn amplify the urban heat island effect in cities.[\[12\]](#cite_note-:1-12): 993  Compact and dense [urban development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_Development "Urban Development") may also increase the urban heat island effect, leading to higher temperatures and increased [exposure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultraviolet_index "Ultraviolet index").[\[13\]](#cite_note-13)
642: 
643: ## Definition
644: 
645: \[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Urban_heat_island&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Definition")\]
646: 
647: A definition of *urban heat island* is: "The relative warmth of a city compared with surrounding rural areas."[\[14\]](#cite_note-:4-14): 2926  This relative warmth is caused by "heat trapping due to land use, the configuration and design of the [built environment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Built_environment "Built environment"), including street layout and building size, the heat-absorbing properties of urban [building materials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Building_material "Building material"), reduced ventilation, reduced greenery and water features, and domestic and industrial heat emissions generated directly from human activities".[\[14\]](#cite_note-:4-14): 2926 
648:

661: ### Diurnal variability
662: 
663: \[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Urban_heat_island&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Diurnal variability")\]
664: 
665: [![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/91/Urban_heat_island_variation.jpg/500px-Urban_heat_island_variation.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Urban_heat_island_variation.jpg)
666: 
667: Cities often experience stronger urban heat island effects at night; effects can vary with location and topography of metropolitan areas.
668: 
669: Throughout the daytime, particularly when the skies are cloudless, urban surfaces are warmed by the absorption of [solar radiation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_radiation "Solar radiation"). Surfaces in the urban areas tend to warm faster than those of the surrounding rural areas. By virtue of their high [heat capacities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_capacity "Heat capacity"), urban surfaces act as a reservoir of heat energy. For example, concrete can hold roughly 2,000 times as much heat as an equivalent volume of air.[\[15\]](#cite_note-15) "This study shows that urban surfaces such as concrete absorb and store large amounts of heat during the day, confirming the high heat capacity effect described in urban heat islands." As a result, high daytime surface temperatures within the UHI can be easily seen via thermal [remote sensing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remote_sensing "Remote sensing"). As is often the case with daytime heating, this warming also has the effect of generating [convective](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_convection "Atmospheric convection") winds within the urban [boundary layer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_boundary_layer "Planetary boundary layer"). At night, the situation reverses. The absence of solar heating leads to the decrease of atmospheric convection and the stabilization of urban boundary layer. If enough stabilization occurs, an [inversion layer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inversion_\(meteorology\) "Inversion (meteorology)") is formed. This traps urban air near the surface, keeping surface air warm from the still-warm urban surfaces, resulting in warmer nighttime air temperatures within the UHI.
670: 
671: Generally speaking, the difference in temperature between the urban and surrounding rural area is more pronounced at night than in daytime.[\[16\]](#cite_note-16) For example, in the United States, the temperature in urban areas tends to be warmer than the surrounding area by about 1–7 °F (0.55–3.9 °C) during the daytime, and about 2–5 °F (1.1–2.8 °C) warmer at night.[\[17\]](#cite_note-:22-17) However, the difference is more pronounced during the day in arid climates such as those in southeastern China and Taiwan.[\[18\]](#cite_note-18)[\[19\]](#cite_note-19) Studies have shown that diurnal variability is impacted by several factors including local climate and weather, seasonality, humidity, vegetation, surfaces, and materials in the built environment.[\[20\]](#cite_note-20)[\[17\]](#cite_note-:22-17)[\[21\]](#cite_note-21)[\[22\]](#cite_note-22)
672: 
673: ### Seasonal variability
674: 
675: \[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Urban_heat_island&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Seasonal variability")\]
676: 
677: Seasonal variability is less well understood than diurnal variability of the urban heat island temperature difference.[\[23\]](#cite_note-:8-23) Complex relationships between precipitation, vegetation, solar radiation, and surface materials in various local climate zones play interlocking roles that influence seasonal patterns of temperature variation in a particular urban heat island.[\[23\]](#cite_note-:8-23)[\[24\]](#cite_note-24)[\[25\]](#cite_note-25)[\[26\]](#cite_note-26)
678: 
679: ## Measurements and predictions
680: 
681: \[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Urban_heat_island&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Measurements and predictions")\]
682: 
683: ### Urban Heat Island Index (UHII)
684: 
685: \[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Urban_heat_island&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Urban Heat Island Index (UHII)")\]
686: 
687: One method to quantify the UHI effect within urban areas is the UHI Index created by the [Californian EPA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Environmental_Protection_Agency "California Environmental Protection Agency") in 2015. It compares the temperature of a surveyed area and rural reference points upwind from the surveyed area, at a height of two meters above ground level. The difference in temperature in degrees [Celsius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celsius "Celsius") is taken hourly and differences with an increased urban temperature compared to the reference points are summed up, creating a number of degree-Celsius-hours, which is the UHI Index of the surveyed area. The measure of Celsius-hours might be averaged over many days, but is specified as Celsius-hours per averaged day.[\[27\]](#cite_note-27)[\[28\]](#cite_note-:6-28)[\[29\]](#cite_note-:7-29)
688: 
689: The index was created to estimate the expected use of air conditioning and resulting [greenhouse gas emissions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenhouse_gas_emissions "Greenhouse gas emissions") in California.[\[28\]](#cite_note-:6-28) The index does not consider values of or differences in wind-speed, humidity, or [solar influx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_irradiance "Solar irradiance"), which might influence [perceived temperature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apparent_temperature "Apparent temperature") or the operation of air conditioners.[\[29\]](#cite_note-:7-29)
690: 
691: ### Models and simulations
692: 
693: \[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Urban_heat_island&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Models and simulations")\]
694: 
695: If a city or [town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Town "Town") has a good system of taking weather observations the UHI can be measured directly.[\[30\]](#cite_note-30) An alternative is to use a complex simulation of the location to calculate the UHI, or to use an approximate empirical method.[\[31\]](#cite_note-31)[\[32\]](#cite_note-32) Such models allow the UHI to be included in estimates of future temperatures rises within cities due to climate change.
696: 
697: Leonard O. Myrup published the first comprehensive numerical treatment to predict the effects of the urban heat island (UHI) in 1969.[\[33\]](#cite_note-:3-33) The heat island effect was found to be the net result of several competing physical processes. In general, reduced evaporation in the city center and the thermal properties of the city building and paving materials are the dominant parameters.[\[33\]](#cite_note-:3-33) Modern simulation environments include [ENVI-met](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ENVI-met "ENVI-met"), which simulates all interactions between building and ground surfaces, plants and ambient air.[\[34\]](#cite_note-34)

Example of dense urban living without green spaces which leads to a pronounced urban heat island effect ([Milan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milan "Milan"), Italy)

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ee/New_York_City-Manhattan-Central_Park_%28Gentry%29.jpg/330px-New_York_City-Manhattan-Central_Park_%28Gentry%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:New_York_City-Manhattan-Central_Park_\(Gentry\).jpg)

Example of an inner city green space, which can reduce the urban heat island effect ([Central Park, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Park,_New_York "Central Park, New York"))

The **urban heat island** (**UHI**) effect is a [meteorological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meteorology "Meteorology") and [climatological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climatology "Climatology") phenomenon in which [urban areas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_areas "Urban areas") experience significantly warmer temperatures than surrounding [rural areas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rural_areas "Rural areas"). The [temperature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temperature "Temperature") difference is usually larger at night than during the day,[\[1\]](#cite_note-Phelan-1) and is most apparent when [winds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wind "Wind") are weak, under [block](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Block_\(meteorology\) "Block (meteorology)") conditions, noticeably during the [summer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer "Summer") and [winter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winter "Winter"). The main cause of the UHI effect is from the modification of land surfaces, while [waste heat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waste_heat "Waste heat") generated by energy usage is a secondary contributor.[\[2\]](#cite_note-dx.doi.org-2)[\[3\]](#cite_note-3)[\[4\]](#cite_note-liyan2012-4) Urban areas occupy about 0.5% of the Earth's land surface but host more than half of the world's population.[\[5\]](#cite_note-5) As a population center grows, it tends to expand its area and increase its average temperature. Another key term is **heat island**; the term can be used to refer to any area that is relatively hotter than the surroundings, but generally refers to human-disturbed areas.[\[6\]](#cite_note-6)

Monthly [rainfall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Precipitation_\(meteorology\) "Precipitation (meteorology)") is greater downwind of cities, partially due to the UHI. Increases in heat within urban centers increase the length of [growing seasons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Growing_season "Growing season"), decrease [air quality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_quality "Air quality") by increasing the production of pollutants such as [ozone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozone "Ozone"), and decrease water quality as warmer waters flow into area streams and put stress on their [ecosystems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecosystem "Ecosystem").

Not all cities have a distinct urban heat island, and the heat island characteristics depend strongly on the background climate of the area where the [city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City "City") is located.[\[7\]](#cite_note-SUE-7) The impact in a city can significantly change based on its local environment. Heat can be reduced by [tree cover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forest_cover "Forest cover") and [green space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_green_space "Urban green space"), which act as sources of shade and promote [evaporative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evapotranspiration "Evapotranspiration") cooling.[\[8\]](#cite_note-Waldrop-8) Other options include [green roofs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_roof "Green roof"), [passive daytime radiative cooling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passive_daytime_radiative_cooling "Passive daytime radiative cooling") applications, ventilation corridors, the [use of lighter-colored surfaces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reflective_surfaces_\(climate_engineering\) "Reflective surfaces (climate engineering)"), and less absorptive building materials. These reflect more [sunlight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunlight "Sunlight") and absorb less heat.[\[9\]](#cite_note-9)[\[10\]](#cite_note-:2-10)[\[11\]](#cite_note-:13-11)

[Climate change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change "Climate change") is not the cause of urban heat islands, but it is causing more frequent and more intense [heat waves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_wave "Heat wave"), which in turn amplify the urban heat island effect in cities.[\[12\]](#cite_note-:1-12): 993  Compact and dense [urban development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_Development "Urban Development") may also increase the urban heat island effect, leading to higher temperatures and increased [exposure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultraviolet_index "Ultraviolet index").[\[13\]](#cite_note-13)

## Definition

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Urban_heat_island&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Definition")\]

A definition of *urban heat island* is: "The relative warmth of a city compared with surrounding rural areas."[\[14\]](#cite_note-:4-14): 2926  This relative warmth is caused by "heat trapping due to land use, the configuration and design of the [built environment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Built_environment "Built environment"), including street layout and building size, the heat-absorbing properties of urban [building materials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Building_material "Building material"), reduced ventilation, reduced greenery and water features, and domestic and industrial heat emissions generated directly from human activities".[\[14\]](#cite_note-:4-14): 2926 

## Description

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Urban_heat_island&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Description")\]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/Urban_heat_island.svg/500px-Urban_heat_island.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Urban_heat_island.svg)

Mechanism of the urban heat island effect: the densely-built [downtown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downtown "Downtown") areas tend to be warmer than suburban residential areas or rural areas.

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ce/HeatIsland_Kanto_en.png/500px-HeatIsland_Kanto_en.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:HeatIsland_Kanto_en.png)

### Diurnal variability

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Urban_heat_island&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Diurnal variability")\]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/91/Urban_heat_island_variation.jpg/500px-Urban_heat_island_variation.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Urban_heat_island_variation.jpg)

Cities often experience stronger urban heat island effects at night; effects can vary with location and topography of metropolitan areas.

Throughout the daytime, particularly when the skies are cloudless, urban surfaces are warmed by the absorption of [solar radiation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_radiation "Solar radiation"). Surfaces in the urban areas tend to warm faster than those of the surrounding rural areas. By virtue of their high [heat capacities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_capacity "Heat capacity"), urban surfaces act as a reservoir of heat energy. For example, concrete can hold roughly 2,000 times as much heat as an equivalent volume of air.[\[15\]](#cite_note-15) "This study shows that urban surfaces such as concrete absorb and store large amounts of heat during the day, confirming the high heat capacity effect described in urban heat islands." As a result, high daytime surface temperatures within the UHI can be easily seen via thermal [remote sensing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remote_sensing "Remote sensing"). As is often the case with daytime heating, this warming also has the effect of generating [convective](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_convection "Atmospheric convection") winds within the urban [boundary layer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_boundary_layer "Planetary boundary layer"). At night, the situation reverses. The absence of solar heating leads to the decrease of atmospheric convection and the stabilization of urban boundary layer. If enough stabilization occurs, an [inversion layer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inversion_\(meteorology\) "Inversion (meteorology)") is formed. This traps urban air near the surface, keeping surface air warm from the still-warm urban surfaces, resulting in warmer nighttime air temperatures within the UHI.

Generally speaking, the difference in temperature between the urban and surrounding rural area is more pronounced at night than in daytime.[\[16\]](#cite_note-16) For example, in the United States, the temperature in urban areas tends to be warmer than the surrounding area by about 1–7 °F (0.55–3.9 °C) during the daytime, and about 2–5 °F (1.1–2.8 °C) warmer at night.[\[17\]](#cite_note-:22-17) However, the difference is more pronounced during the day in arid climates such as those in southeastern China and Taiwan.[\[18\]](#cite_note-18)[\[19\]](#cite_note-19) Studies have shown that diurnal variability is impacted by several factors including local climate and weather, seasonality, humidity, vegetation, surfaces, and materials in the built environment.[\[20\]](#cite_note-20)[\[17\]](#cite_note-:22-17)[\[21\]](#cite_note-21)[\[22\]](#cite_note-22)

### Seasonal variability

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Urban_heat_island&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Seasonal variability")\]

Seasonal variability is less well understood than diurnal variability of the urban heat island temperature difference.[\[23\]](#cite_note-:8-23) Complex relationships between precipitation, vegetation, solar radiation, and surface materials in various local climate zones play interlocking roles that influence seasonal patterns of temperature variation in a particular urban heat island.[\[23\]](#cite_note-:8-23)[\[24\]](#cite_note-24)[\[25\]](#cite_note-25)[\[26\]](#cite_note-26)

## Measurements and predictions

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Urban_heat_island&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Measurements and predictions")\]

### Urban Heat Island Index (UHII)

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Urban_heat_island&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Urban Heat Island Index (UHII)")\]

One method to quantify the UHI effect within urban areas is the UHI Index created by the [Californian EPA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Environmental_Protection_Agency "California Environmental Protection Agency") in 2015. It compares the temperature of a surveyed area and rural reference points upwind from the surveyed area, at a height of two meters above ground level. The difference in temperature in degrees [Celsius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celsius "Celsius") is taken hourly and differences with an increased urban temperature compared to the reference points are summed up, creating a number of degree-Celsius-hours, which is the UHI Index of the surveyed area. The measure of Celsius-hours might be averaged over many days, but is specified as Celsius-hours per averaged day.[\[27\]](#cite_note-27)[\[28\]](#cite_note-:6-28)[\[29\]](#cite_note-:7-29)

The index was created to estimate the expected use of air conditioning and resulting [greenhouse gas emissions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenhouse_gas_emissions "Greenhouse gas emissions") in California.[\[28\]](#cite_note-:6-28) The index does not consider values of or differences in wind-speed, humidity, or [solar influx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_irradiance "Solar irradiance"), which might influence [perceived temperature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apparent_temperature "Apparent temperature") or the operation of air conditioners.[\[29\]](#cite_note-:7-29)

### Models and simulations

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Urban_heat_island&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Models and simulations")\]

If a city or [town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Town "Town") has a good system of taking weather observations the UHI can be measured directly.[\[30\]](#cite_note-30) An alternative is to use a complex simulation of the location to calculate the UHI, or to use an approximate empirical method.[\[31\]](#cite_note-31)[\[32\]](#cite_note-32) Such models allow the UHI to be included in estimates of future temperatures rises within cities due to climate change.

Leonard O. Myrup published the first comprehensive numerical treatment to predict the effects of the urban heat island (UHI) in 1969.[\[33\]](#cite_note-:3-33) The heat island effect was found to be the net result of several competing physical processes. In general, reduced evaporation in the city center and the thermal properties of the city building and paving materials are the dominant parameters.[\[33\]](#cite_note-:3-33) Modern simulation environments include [ENVI-met](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ENVI-met "ENVI-met"), which simulates all interactions between building and ground surfaces, plants and ambient air.[\[34\]](#cite_note-34)

719: There are several causes of an urban heat island (UHI) related to common [urban design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_design "Urban design") aspects. For example, dark surfaces absorb significantly more [solar radiation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_radiation "Solar radiation"), which causes urban concentrations of roads and buildings to heat more than suburban and rural areas during the day;[\[2\]](#cite_note-dx.doi.org-2) materials commonly used in urban areas for pavement and roofs, such as [concrete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concrete "Concrete") and [asphalt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asphalt_concrete "Asphalt concrete"), have significantly different thermal bulk properties (including [heat capacity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Specific_heat_capacity "Specific heat capacity") and [thermal conductivity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermal_conductivity "Thermal conductivity")) and surface radiative properties ([albedo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albedo "Albedo") and [emissivity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emissivity "Emissivity")) than the surrounding rural areas. This causes a change in the [energy budget](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_energy_budget "Earth's energy budget") of the urban area, often leading to higher temperatures than surrounding rural areas.[\[35\]](#cite_note-Okeljnljn-35)
720: 
721: [Pavements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pavers_\(flooring\) "Pavers (flooring)"), [parking lots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parking_lot "Parking lot"), roads or, more generally speaking [transport infrastructure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transport_infrastructure "Transport infrastructure"), contribute significantly to the urban heat island effect.[\[36\]](#cite_note-:5-36) For example, pavement infrastructure is a main contributor to urban heat during summer afternoons in [Phoenix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix,_Arizona "Phoenix, Arizona"), United States.[\[36\]](#cite_note-:5-36)
722: 
723: Another major reason is the lack of [evapotranspiration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evapotranspiration "Evapotranspiration") (for example, through lack of vegetation) in urban areas.[\[37\]](#cite_note-37) The U.S. Forest Service found in 2018 that cities in the United States are losing 36 million trees each year.[\[38\]](#cite_note-38) With a decreased amount of vegetation, cities also lose the shade and evaporative cooling effect of trees.[\[39\]](#cite_note-39)[\[40\]](#cite_note-40)
724: 
725: Other causes of a UHI are due to geometric effects. The tall buildings within many urban areas provide multiple surfaces for the reflection and absorption of sunlight, increasing the efficiency with which urban areas are heated. This is called the "[urban canyon effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_canyon "Urban canyon")". Another effect of buildings is the blocking of wind, which also inhibits cooling by [convection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convection "Convection") and prevents pollutants from dissipating. Waste heat from automobiles, air conditioning, industry, and other sources also contribute to the UHI.[\[4\]](#cite_note-liyan2012-4)[\[41\]](#cite_note-41)[\[42\]](#cite_note-42)
726: 
727: Heat islands can be affected by proximity to different types of land cover, so that proximity to barren land causes urban land to become hotter and proximity to vegetation makes it cooler.[\[43\]](#cite_note-43)
728: 
729: ### Poor landscaping
730: 
731: \[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Urban_heat_island&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Poor landscaping")\]
732: 
733: The design of personal landscapes like yards and public areas like city parks can have a large effect on UHIs. A well designed landscape built around [native plants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_species "Native species") can survive with natural rainfall and will be resilient to heat waves and excessive heat from parking lots. These landscapes provide shade, stability, and moisture to the surrounding areas. Lawns of non-native grasses will not be resilient against changes in climate, temperature, rainfall, or water availability. Large unbroken parking lots can heat up much hotter than surrounding areas.[\[44\]](#cite_note-44) Factoring in space for tree cover, shade structures, and resilient plants can prevent a development from becoming dangerously hot or contributing to UHIs.[\[45\]](#cite_note-45)
734: 
735: ### Air pollution
736: 
737: \[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Urban_heat_island&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Air pollution")\]
738: 
739: High levels of [air pollution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_pollution "Air pollution") in urban areas can also increase the UHI, as many forms of pollution change the radiative properties of the atmosphere.[\[35\]](#cite_note-Okeljnljn-35) UHI not only raises urban temperatures but also increases ozone concentrations because ozone is a [greenhouse gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenhouse_gas "Greenhouse gas") whose formation will accelerate with the increase of temperature.[\[46\]](#cite_note-46)
740: 
741: ### Climate change as an amplifier
742: 
743: \[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Urban_heat_island&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Climate change as an amplifier")\]
744: 
745: Further information: [Climate change and cities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change_and_cities "Climate change and cities") and [Climate change adaptation § Heat waves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change_adaptation#Heat_waves "Climate change adaptation")
746: 
747: Climate change is not a cause but an amplifier of the urban heat island effect. The [IPCC Sixth Assessment Report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IPCC_Sixth_Assessment_Report "IPCC Sixth Assessment Report") from 2022 summarized the available research accordingly: "Climate change increases [heat stress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_stress "Heat stress") risks in cities \[...\] and amplifies the urban heat island across Asian cities at 1.5 °C and 2 °C warming levels, both substantially larger than under present climates \[...\]."[\[47\]](#cite_note-47): 66 
748: 
749: The report goes on to say: "In a warming world, increasing air temperature makes the urban heat island effect in cities worse. One key risk is [heatwaves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_wave "Heat wave") in cities that are likely to affect half of the future global urban population, with negative impacts on human health and economic productivity."[\[12\]](#cite_note-:1-12): 993 
750: 
751: These interactions between heat and built infrastructures also increase the risk of heat stress for people living in cities.[\[12\]](#cite_note-:1-12): 993 
752: 
753: ### Increased urbanization
754: 
755: \[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Urban_heat_island&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Increased urbanization")\]
756: 
757: Increased [urbanization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urbanization "Urbanization") is a major leading cause for increased urban heat risks, as it replaces vegetated areas with impervious surfaces and concentrates people into smaller land areas.[\[48\]](#cite_note-:2a-48) There are measurable and designable factors that determine if an urban or suburban area will have a heat island effect. Suburban areas usually have more greenery but can be subject to rapid heating if drought conditions result in there not being enough water for private [lawns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawn "Lawn"). Suburban areas also [sprawl out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_sprawl "Urban sprawl") faster and if [car-dependant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Car_dependency "Car dependency"), require large amounts of asphalt and large parking lots which heat up quick and retain heat. Cities are more likely to have UHIs but can be designed to have tall towers surrounded by large parks which can exist harmoniously with the surrounding climate.
758: 
759: #### Spatial distribution
760: 
761: \[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Urban_heat_island&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Spatial distribution")\]
762: 
763: Historic urbanization processes, such as [redlining](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redlining "Redlining") in the United States, have lasting impacts on land use and may perpetuate disparities in urban heat through unequal distribution of vegetation.[\[49\]](#cite_note-:0-49)[\[50\]](#cite_note-:3a-50) Access to healthcare, public transportation, adequate housing, and reliable energy typically govern disparities to heat, of which many of these communities may lack access to.[\[50\]](#cite_note-:3a-50) Such differences in spatial distribution leave certain, localized neighborhood at risk for micro urban heat islands.[\[51\]](#cite_note-:4a-51) Socially vulnerable groups are known to live in more densely populated areas with little vegetation that in turn have higher threats to heat exposure and often have adapting to and mitigation their exposure.[\[51\]](#cite_note-:4a-51)
764: 
765: #### Housing conditions
766: 
767: \[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Urban_heat_island&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Housing conditions")\]
768: 
769: Housing conditions are a factor that contributes to urban heat inequity. Living on the top-floor, having a home with a dark roof, and poor insulation exacerbate heating conditions during hot weather.[\[52\]](#cite_note-:1a-52) Lower income individuals may also not have access to air-conditioning or be unable to afford the increased electricity usage.[\[52\]](#cite_note-:1a-52) In condensed cities, opening the windows for airflow and cooler air could introduce air pollution and odor into the home.[\[52\]](#cite_note-:1a-52) High-density housing in Asia often has constraints on building updates that promote cooling.[\[52\]](#cite_note-:1a-52)
770: 
771: #### Space poverty
772: 
773: \[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Urban_heat_island&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Space poverty")\]
774: 
775: Another contributor to inequality is space poverty, which refers to a significantly reduced indoor residential space in a home.[\[52\]](#cite_note-:1a-52) Space poverty is a significant issue in Hong Kong, where low-income individuals live in extremely small, sub-divided units, which has led to overcrowding and indoor air pollution.[\[52\]](#cite_note-:1a-52) The units promote little movement, and all furniture, kitchen appliances, and bathroom necessities must fit into one sub-divided room.[\[52\]](#cite_note-:1a-52) These units are typically developed from derelict buildings that have poor ventilation and less access to proper space cooling.[\[52\]](#cite_note-:1a-52) High-density housing in Asia often has constraints on building updates that promote cooling, and residents often lack the space and authority to complete any improvements to their condition.[\[52\]](#cite_note-:1a-52) These residents typically seek out adequate [third places](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_place "Third place"), such as libraries, parks, and cafés, to access proper cooling and space.[\[52\]](#cite_note-:1a-52)
776: 
777: ## Impacts
778: 
779: \[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Urban_heat_island&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Impacts")\]
780: 
781: [![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/43/Dubai_skyline_2015_%28crop%29.jpg/250px-Dubai_skyline_2015_%28crop%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dubai_skyline_2015_\(crop\).jpg)
782: 
783: Example of urbanization: [Dubai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dubai "Dubai")
784: 
785: ### On weather and climate
786: 
787: \[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Urban_heat_island&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: On weather and climate")\]
788: 
789: Aside from the effect on temperature, UHIs can produce secondary effects on local meteorology, including the altering of local wind patterns, the development of [clouds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloud "Cloud") and [fog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fog "Fog"), the [humidity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humidity "Humidity"), and the rates of precipitation.[\[53\]](#cite_note-53) The extra heat provided by the UHI leads to greater upward motion, which can induce additional shower and thunderstorm activity. In addition, the UHI creates during the day a local low pressure area where relatively moist air from its rural surroundings converges, possibly leading to more favorable conditions for cloud formation.[\[54\]](#cite_note-Hee-54) Rainfall rates downwind of cities are increased between 48% and 116%. Partly as a result of this warming, monthly rainfall is about 28% greater between 20 and 40 miles (32 and 64 km) downwind of cities, compared with upwind.[\[55\]](#cite_note-55) Some cities show a total precipitation increase of 51%.[\[56\]](#cite_note-56)
790: 
791: One study concluded that cities change the climate in area two–four times larger than their own area.[\[57\]](#cite_note-57) One 1999 comparison between urban and rural areas proposed that urban heat island effects have little influence on [global mean temperature trends](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instrumental_temperature_record "Instrumental temperature record").[\[58\]](#cite_note-58) Others suggested that urban heat islands affect global climate by impacting the jet stream.[\[59\]](#cite_note-59)
792: 
793: ### On human health
794: 
795: \[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Urban_heat_island&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: On human health")\]
796: 
797: See also: [Heat illness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_illness "Heat illness") and [Effects of climate change on human health § Higher global temperatures and heat waves (direct risk)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effects_of_climate_change_on_human_health#Higher_global_temperatures_and_heat_waves_\(direct_risk\) "Effects of climate change on human health")
798: 
799: [![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0a/Atlanta_thermal.jpg/330px-Atlanta_thermal.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Atlanta_thermal.jpg)
800: 
801: Image of [Atlanta, Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta "Atlanta"), showing temperature distribution, with blue showing cool temperatures, red warm, and hot areas appear white
802: 
803: UHIs have the potential to directly influence the health and welfare of urban residents. As UHIs are characterized by increased temperature, they can potentially increase the magnitude and duration of heat waves within cities. The number of individuals exposed to extreme temperatures is increased by the UHI-induced warming.[\[60\]](#cite_note-60) The nighttime effect of UHIs can be particularly harmful during a heat wave, as it deprives urban residents of the cool relief found in rural areas during the night.[\[61\]](#cite_note-Clarke-61) Exposure to extreme urban heat can increase the risk of heat-related illnesses and mortality, particularly among elderly populations.[\[62\]](#cite_note-62)
804: 
805: Increased temperatures have been reported to cause [heat illnesses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_illness "Heat illness"), such as [heat stroke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_stroke "Heat stroke"), [heat exhaustion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_exhaustion "Heat exhaustion"), [heat syncope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_syncope "Heat syncope"), and [heat cramps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_cramps "Heat cramps").[\[63\]](#cite_note-Review1-63)
806: 
807: Extreme heat is the deadliest form of weather in the U.S. Per a study by Professor Terri Adams-Fuller, heat waves kill more people in the U.S. than hurricanes, floods, and tornadoes combined.[\[64\]](#cite_note-64) These heat illnesses are more common within medium-to-large metro areas than the rest of the U.S., largely in part due to UHIs. Heat illnesses can also be compounded when combined with air pollution which is common in many urban areas.[\[65\]](#cite_note-65)
808: 
809: Heat exposure can have adverse effects on mental health. Increases in temperature can contribute to increased aggression, as well as more cases of domestic violence and substance abuse.[\[66\]](#cite_note-66) Greater heat can also negatively impact school performance and education. According to a study by Hyunkuk Cho of Yeungnam University, an increased number of days with extreme heat each year correlates to a decrease in student test scores.[\[67\]](#cite_note-67)
810: 
811: High UHI intensity correlates with increased concentrations of air pollutants that gathered at night, which can affect the next day's [air quality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_pollution "Air pollution").[\[68\]](#cite_note-DOE-68) These pollutants include [volatile organic compounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volatile_organic_compounds "Volatile organic compounds"), [carbon monoxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_monoxide "Carbon monoxide"), [nitrogen oxides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen_oxides "Nitrogen oxides"), and [particulate matter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Particulates "Particulates").[\[69\]](#cite_note-WHO-69) The production of these pollutants combined with the higher temperatures in UHIs can quicken the production of [ozone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozone "Ozone").[\[68\]](#cite_note-DOE-68) Ozone at surface level is considered to be a harmful pollutant.[\[68\]](#cite_note-DOE-68) Studies suggest that increased temperatures in UHIs can increase polluted days but also note that other factors (e.g. [air pressure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_pressure "Atmospheric pressure"), [cloud cover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloud_cover "Cloud cover"), [wind speed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wind_speed "Wind speed")) can also have an effect on pollution.[\[68\]](#cite_note-DOE-68)
812: 
813: Studies from [Hong Kong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong "Hong Kong") have found that areas of the city with poorer outdoor urban air ventilation tended to have stronger urban heat island effects[\[70\]](#cite_note-70) and had significantly higher all-cause mortality[\[71\]](#cite_note-71) compared to areas with better ventilation. Another study in [Babol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babol,_Mazandaran "Babol, Mazandaran"), Iran saw an increase in Surface Urban Heat Island Intensity (SUHII) from the year 1985 to 2017.[\[72\]](#cite_note-72) Surface UHI's are more prominent during the day and are measured using the land surface temperature and remote sensing.[\[73\]](#cite_note-73)
814: 
815: Heat stress vulnerability refers to an individual's predisposition, typically due to demographic factors, to be negatively impacted by heat.[\[52\]](#cite_note-:1a-52) The measurement takes into account daily routines, location, sensitivity due to demographic factors, including age.[\[52\]](#cite_note-:1a-52) Some demographic groups known to have higher heat stress vulnerability include the elderly, women, children, low-income households, and those who are chronically ill.[\[52\]](#cite_note-:1a-52) Elderly populations are included because they are often unable to regulate their body temperatures and typically have pre-existing medical conditions that make them more susceptible to heat.[\[52\]](#cite_note-:1a-52) Children are also sensitive to increased heat, which may cause stress on their developing bodies.[\[52\]](#cite_note-:1a-52) Intensified indoor heat causes stress on the mind and body and strains domestic relations.[\[52\]](#cite_note-:1a-52)
816: 
817: ### On water bodies and aquatic organisms
818: 
819: \[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Urban_heat_island&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: On water bodies and aquatic organisms")\]
820: 
821: UHIs also impair [water quality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_quality "Water quality"). Hot pavement and rooftop surfaces transfer their excess heat to [stormwater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stormwater "Stormwater"), which then drains into storm sewers and raises water temperatures as it is released into streams, rivers, ponds, and lakes. Additionally, increased urban water body temperatures lead to a [decrease in biodiversity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biodiversity_loss "Biodiversity loss") in the water.[\[74\]](#cite_note-74) For example, in August 2001, rains over [Cedar Rapids, Iowa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_Rapids,_Iowa "Cedar Rapids, Iowa") led to a 10.5 °C (18.9 °F) rise in the nearby stream within one hour, resulting in a [fish kill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fish_kill "Fish kill") which affected an estimated 188 fish.[\[75\]](#cite_note-75) Since the temperature of the rain was comparatively cool, the deaths could be attributed to the hot pavement of the city. Similar events have been documented across the American Midwest, as well as Oregon and California.[\[76\]](#cite_note-76) Rapid temperature changes can be stressful to aquatic ecosystems.[\[77\]](#cite_note-77)
822: 
823: With the temperature of the nearby buildings sometimes reaching a difference of over 50 °F (28 °C) from the near-surface air temperature, precipitation warms rapidly, and [run-off](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_runoff "Urban runoff") into nearby streams, lakes and rivers (or other bodies of water) to provide excessive [thermal pollution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermal_pollution "Thermal pollution"). The increase in thermal pollution has the potential to increase water temperature by 20 to 30 °F (11 to 17 °C). This increase causes the fish species inhabiting the body of water to undergo thermal stress and shock due to the rapid change in temperature of their habitat.[\[78\]](#cite_note-78)
824: 
825: [Permeable pavements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permeable_paving "Permeable paving") may reduce these effects by [percolating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percolation "Percolation") water through the pavement into subsurface storage areas where it can be dissipated through absorption and evaporation.[\[79\]](#cite_note-coolpave-79)
826: 
827: UHIs can both worsen and be worsened by [droughts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drought "Drought").\[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*\][\[80\]](#cite_note-80)
828: 
829: ### On animals
830: 
831: \[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Urban_heat_island&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: On animals")\]
832: 
833: Species that are good at colonizing can use conditions provided by urban heat islands to thrive in regions outside of their normal range. Examples of this include the [grey-headed flying fox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grey-headed_flying_fox "Grey-headed flying fox") (*Pteropus poliocephalus*) and the [common house gecko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_house_gecko "Common house gecko") (*Hemidactylus frenatus*).[\[81\]](#cite_note-Paige_S_2005-81) Grey-headed flying foxes, found in [Melbourne, Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melbourne,_Australia "Melbourne, Australia"), colonized urban habitats following the increase in temperatures there. Increased temperatures, causing warmer winter conditions, made the city more similar in climate to the more northerly wildland habitat of the species.
834: 
835: With temperate climates, urban heat islands will extend the growing season, therefore altering breeding strategies of inhabiting species.[\[81\]](#cite_note-Paige_S_2005-81) This can be best observed in the effects that urban heat islands have on water temperature (see [effects on water bodies](#on_water_bodies_and_aquatic_organisms)).
836: 
837: Urban heat islands caused by cities have altered the [natural selection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_selection "Natural selection") process.[\[81\]](#cite_note-Paige_S_2005-81) Selective pressures like temporal variation in food, predation and water are relaxed causing a new set of selective forces to roll out. For example, within urban habitats, insects are more abundant than in rural areas. Insects are [ectotherms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ectotherms "Ectotherms"). This means that they depend on the temperature of the environment to control their body temperature, making the warmer climates of the city perfect for their ability to thrive. A study done in [Raleigh, North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raleigh,_North_Carolina "Raleigh, North Carolina") conducted on *[Parthenolecanium quercifex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parthenolecanium_quercifex "Parthenolecanium quercifex")* (oak scales), showed that this particular species preferred warmer climates and were therefore found in higher abundance in urban habitats than on [oak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oak "Oak") trees in rural habitats. Over time spent living in urban habitats, they have adapted to thrive in warmer climates than in cooler ones.[\[82\]](#cite_note-82)
838: 
839: ### On energy usage for cooling
840: 
841: \[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Urban_heat_island&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: On energy usage for cooling")\]
842: 
843: [![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fb/NASA_SLC_Urban_Heat_Island_Effect_Roof.jpg/500px-NASA_SLC_Urban_Heat_Island_Effect_Roof.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:NASA_SLC_Urban_Heat_Island_Effect_Roof.jpg)
844: 
845: Images of [Salt Lake City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt_Lake_City "Salt Lake City") show positive correlation between white reflective roofs and cooler temperatures. Image A depicts an aerial view of Salt Lake City, Utah, site of 865000 sqft white reflective roof. Image B is a thermal infrared image of same area, showing hot (red and yellow) and cool (green and blue) spots. The reflective vinyl roof, not absorbing solar radiation, is shown in blue surrounded by other hot spots.
846: 
847: Another consequence of urban heat islands is the increased energy required for [air conditioning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_conditioning "Air conditioning") and [refrigeration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refrigeration "Refrigeration") in cities that are in comparatively hot climates. The heat island effect costs [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles") about [US$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US$ "US$") 100 million per year in energy (in the year 2000).[\[83\]](#cite_note-83) Through the implementation of heat island reduction strategies, significant annual net energy savings have been calculated for northern locations such as Chicago, Salt Lake City, and Toronto.[\[84\]](#cite_note-84)
848: 
849: Every year in the U.S. 15% of energy goes towards the [air conditioning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_conditioning "Air conditioning") of buildings in these urban heat islands. It was reported in 1998 that "the air conditioning demand has risen 10% within the last 40 years."[\[85\]](#cite_note-Rosenfeld98-85)
850: 
851: Increases in air conditioning use also serve to worsen the effects of UHIs at night. While cooler nights are often a reprieve from heat waves during the day, the residual heat created by the use of air conditioning systems can lead to higher nighttime temperatures. According to a study by Professor Francisco Salamanca Palou and colleagues, this residual heat can cause nighttime increases of up to 1 °C in urban areas.[\[86\]](#cite_note-86) Increased energy use from air conditioners also contributes to carbon emissions, which doubly exacerbates the effects of UHIs.
852: 
853: ## Options for reducing heat island effects
854: 
855: \[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Urban_heat_island&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Options for reducing heat island effects")\]
856: 
857: [![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f7/Ogr%C3%B3d_botaniczny_UMCS.png/250px-Ogr%C3%B3d_botaniczny_UMCS.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ogród_botaniczny_UMCS.png)
858: 
859: Botanical Garden in [Lublin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lublin "Lublin"), Poland
860: 
861: Strategies to improve [urban resilience](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_resilience "Urban resilience") by reducing excessive heat in cities include: Planting trees in cities, [cool roofs (painted white or with reflective coating)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reflective_surfaces_\(climate_engineering\) "Reflective surfaces (climate engineering)") and light-coloured concrete, [green infrastructure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_infrastructure "Green infrastructure") (including [green roofs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_roof "Green roof")), [passive daytime radiative cooling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passive_daytime_radiative_cooling "Passive daytime radiative cooling").[\[87\]](#cite_note-87)[\[88\]](#cite_note-auto-88)
862: 
863: The temperature difference between urban areas and the surrounding suburban or rural areas can be as much as 5 °C (9.0 °F). Nearly 40 percent of that increase is due to the prevalence of dark roofs, with the remainder coming from dark-coloured pavement and the declining presence of vegetation. The heat island effect can be counteracted slightly by using white or reflective materials to build houses, roofs, pavements, and roads, thus increasing the overall albedo of the city.[\[89\]](#cite_note-89)
864: 
865: Concentric expansion of cities is unfavourable in terms of the urban heat island phenomenon. It is recommended to plan the development of cities in strips, consistent with the hydrographic network, taking into account green areas with various plant species.[\[90\]](#cite_note-90) In this way, it was planned to build urban settlements stretching over large areas, e.g. [Kielce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kielce "Kielce"), [Szczecin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Szczecin "Szczecin") and [Gdynia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gdynia "Gdynia") in Poland, [Copenhagen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copenhagen "Copenhagen") in Denmark and [Hamburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamburg "Hamburg"), [Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin "Berlin") and [Kiel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiel "Kiel") in Germany.
866: 
867: ### Planting trees in cities
868: 
869: \[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Urban_heat_island&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: Planting trees in cities")\]
870: 
871: Main articles: [Urban forest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_forest "Urban forest") and [Urban forestry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_forestry "Urban forestry")
872: 
873: Planting trees around the city can be another way of increasing albedo and decreasing the urban heat island effect. It is recommended to plant [deciduous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deciduous "Deciduous") trees because they can provide many benefits such as more shade in the summer and not blocking warmth in winter.[\[91\]](#cite_note-Rosenfield97-91) Trees are a necessary feature in combating most of the urban heat island effect because they reduce air temperatures by 10 °F (5.6 °C),[\[92\]](#cite_note-92) and surface temperatures by up to 20–45 °F (11–25 °C).[\[93\]](#cite_note-93) Another benefit of having trees in a city is that trees also help fight global warming by absorbing CO2 from the atmosphere.
874: 
875: Recent syntheses show that increasing street-tree canopy measurably cools pedestrian-level air temperatures, with effects varying by climate, canopy density, and urban form. A 2024 meta-analysis across 110 cities reports typical ~1–2 °C daytime cooling, and a 2024 field study found that locations with no canopy within 10 m were up to five times more likely to exceed 32.2 °C, with air temperature declining linearly as canopy increased.[\[94\]](#cite_note-Li2024-94)[\[95\]](#cite_note-Ettinger2024-95) Tree species diversity and canopy coverage are associated with the cooling effects of urban green spaces, with higher diversity linked to greater temperature reductions in certain seasons.[\[96\]](#cite_note-96)
876: 
877: Urban green infrastructure (UGI) are integrated networks of green spaces in cities and are developed in both private and public areas of the city.[\[49\]](#cite_note-:0-49) Examples of UGI include urban parks with trees and shrub cover, rows of trees along a street, private gardens, rooftop gardens, and other green space throughout a city.[\[52\]](#cite_note-:1a-52) Properly utilized UGI promotes more equitable heat distribution, where improper usage only perpetuates heat inequity.[\[49\]](#cite_note-:0-49) UGI provides shading and [evapotranspiration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evapotranspiration "Evapotranspiration"), which reduces both air and land temperatures.[\[49\]](#cite_note-:0-49) Therefore, a lack of UGI in marginalized communities reduces the land's temperature regulating capabilities promotes heat inequity.[\[49\]](#cite_note-:0-49) UGI is widely recognized as an efficient, sustainable, and non-controversial solution to heat inequity.[\[49\]](#cite_note-:0-49)
878: 
879: ### Cool roofs and light-coloured concrete
880: 
881: \[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Urban_heat_island&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: Cool roofs and light-coloured concrete")\]
882: 
883: Main article: [Reflective surfaces (climate engineering)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reflective_surfaces_\(climate_engineering\) "Reflective surfaces (climate engineering)")
884: 
885: [![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/de/20080708_Chicago_City_Hall_Green_Roof.JPG/250px-20080708_Chicago_City_Hall_Green_Roof.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:20080708_Chicago_City_Hall_Green_Roof.JPG)
886: 
887: Green roof of [Chicago City Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_City_Hall "Chicago City Hall")
888: 
889: Painting rooftops white has become a common strategy to reduce the heat island effect.[\[97\]](#cite_note-autogenerated3-97) In cities, there are many dark coloured surfaces that absorb the heat of the sun in turn lowering the albedo of the city.[\[97\]](#cite_note-autogenerated3-97) White rooftops allow high solar reflectance and high solar emittance, increasing the albedo of the city or area the effect is occurring.[\[97\]](#cite_note-autogenerated3-97) Green roofs and cool roofs can play a big role in helping cities manage extreme heat. In warmer regions, cool roofs were especially effective, with some cutting cooling energy use completely for certain low-rise buildings. Green roofs may be more beneficial in colder climates because they provide insulation and help reduce the need for heating during winter.[\[98\]](#cite_note-98)
890: 
891: Additionally, covering rooftops with a reflective coating has been shown to be an effective measure to reduce solar heat gain. A study led by Oscar Brousse from University College London, which simulated the impact of various cooling measures in London found that rooftops, which were either painted white or had reflective coating, proved to be the most effective solution for reducing outdoor temperatures at the pedestrian level, outperforming solar panels, green roofs, and tree cover. The study simulated the impact of various cooling measures in London during a 2018 heatwave, finding that the so-called cool roofs could reduce average outdoor temperatures by 1.2 °C, and up to 2 °C in certain areas. In comparison, additional tree cover reduced temperatures by 0.3 °C and solar panels by 0.5 °C.[\[88\]](#cite_note-auto-88)
892: 
893: Relative to remedying the other sources of the problem, replacing dark roofing requires the least amount of investment for the most immediate return. A [cool roof](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cool_roof "Cool roof") made from a reflective material such as vinyl reflects at least 75 percent of the sun's rays, and emits at least 70 percent of the solar radiation absorbed by the building envelope. Asphalt built-up roofs (BUR), by comparison, reflect 6 percent to 26 percent of solar radiation.[\[99\]](#cite_note-99)
894: 
895: Using light-coloured concrete has proven effective in reflecting up to 50% more light than asphalt and reducing ambient temperature.[\[100\]](#cite_note-coolpave_2-100) A low albedo value, characteristic of black asphalt, absorbs a large percentage of solar heat creating warmer near-surface temperatures. Paving with light-coloured concrete, in addition to replacing asphalt with light-coloured concrete, communities may be able to lower average temperatures.[\[101\]](#cite_note-worldchange-101) However, research into the interaction between reflective pavements and buildings has found that, unless the nearby buildings are fitted with reflective glass, solar radiation reflected off light-coloured pavements can increase building temperatures, increasing air conditioning demands.[\[102\]](#cite_note-Yaghoobian-102)[\[103\]](#cite_note-103)
896: 
897: There are specific paint formulations for daytime radiative cooling that reflect up to 98.1% of sunlight.[\[104\]](#cite_note-104)[\[105\]](#cite_note-105)
898: 
899: ### Green infrastructure
900: 
901: \[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Urban_heat_island&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: Green infrastructure")\]
902: 
903: Main articles: [Green infrastructure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_infrastructure "Green infrastructure") and [Green roof](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_roof "Green roof")
904: 
905: [![Grassed tramway track in Budapest, Hungary](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/59/Budapest%2C_CAF_Urbos_3%2C_4.jpg/250px-Budapest%2C_CAF_Urbos_3%2C_4.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Budapest,_CAF_Urbos_3,_4.jpg)
906: 
907: [Grassed tramway track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_track "Green track") in Budapest, Hungary
908: 
909: [Green roofs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_roofs "Green roofs") are excellent insulators during the warm weather months and the plants cool the surrounding environment. Plants can improve air quality as they absorb carbon dioxide and concomitantly produce oxygen.[\[106\]](#cite_note-106) Green roofs can also have positive impacts on stormwater management and energy consumption.[\[107\]](#cite_note-107) Cost can be a barrier to implementing a green roof.[\[108\]](#cite_note-108)[\[109\]](#cite_note-:12-109) Several factors influence the cost of a green roof, including design and soil depth, location, and the price of labor and equipment in that market, which is typically lower in more developed markets where there is more experience designing and installing green roofs.[\[110\]](#cite_note-110) The individualized context of each green roof presents a challenge for making broad comparisons and assessments, and focusing only on monetary costs may leave out the social, environmental, and public health benefits green roofs provide.[\[109\]](#cite_note-:12-109) Global comparisons of green roof performance are further challenged by the lack of a shared framework for making such comparisons.[\[109\]](#cite_note-:12-109)
910: 
911: Stormwater management is another option to help mitigate the effect of the urban heat island. Stormwater management controls the water produced by the storm in a way that protects property and infrastructure.[\[111\]](#cite_note-111) Urban infrastructure like streets, sidewalks, and parking lots do not allow for water to penetrate into the earth's surface causing water to flood. By using stormwater management, you can control the flow of the water in ways that can mitigate UHI effect. One way is using a stormwater management technique called pervious pavement system (PPS). This technique has been used in over 30 countries and found to be successful in stormwater management and UHI mitigation. The PPS allows water to flow through the pavement allowing for the water to be absorbed causing the area to be cooled by evaporation.[\[112\]](#cite_note-112)
912: 
913: [Green parking lots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_parking_lot "Green parking lot") use vegetation and surfaces other than asphalt to limit the urban heat island effect.
914: 
915: This section is an excerpt from [Green infrastructure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_infrastructure "Green infrastructure").\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Green_infrastructure&action=edit)\]
916: 
917: [![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dc/Meridian_Hill_Bioswale.jpg/250px-Meridian_Hill_Bioswale.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Meridian_Hill_Bioswale.jpg)
918: 
919: Runoff from the vicinity flows into an adjacent [bioswale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bioswale "Bioswale")
920: 
921: [Green infrastructure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_infrastructure "Green infrastructure") or blue-green infrastructure refers to a network that provides the "ingredients" for solving urban and climatic challenges by building with nature.[\[113\]](#cite_note-Green_infrastructure_Urban_green-blue_grids-113) The main components of this approach include [stormwater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stormwater "Stormwater") management, [climate adaptation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_adaptation "Climate adaptation"), the reduction of [heat stress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_stress "Heat stress"), increasing [biodiversity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biodiversity "Biodiversity"), [food production](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Food_production "Food production"), better [air quality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_quality "Air quality"), [sustainable energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sustainable_energy "Sustainable energy") production, clean water, and [healthy soils](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soil_health "Soil health"), as well as more human centered functions, such as increased [quality of life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quality_of_life "Quality of life") through recreation and the provision of shade and shelter in and around towns and cities.[\[114\]](#cite_note-114)[\[115\]](#cite_note-115) Green infrastructure also serves to provide an ecological framework for social, economic, and environmental health of the surroundings.[\[116\]](#cite_note-Green_infrastructure_issuu.com-116) More recently scholars and activists have also called for green infrastructure that promotes social inclusion and equity rather than reinforcing pre-existing structures of unequal access to nature-based services.[\[117\]](#cite_note-117)
922: 
923: ### Passive daytime radiative cooling
924: 
925: \[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Urban_heat_island&action=edit&section=27 "Edit section: Passive daytime radiative cooling")\]
926: 
927: Main article: [Passive daytime radiative cooling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passive_daytime_radiative_cooling "Passive daytime radiative cooling")
928: 
929: [![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/44/Festividad_del_Corpus_Christi%2C_Toledo%2C_Espa%C3%B1a_-_panoramio.jpg/250px-Festividad_del_Corpus_Christi%2C_Toledo%2C_Espa%C3%B1a_-_panoramio.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Festividad_del_Corpus_Christi,_Toledo,_España_-_panoramio.jpg)
930: 
931: Street awnings Festividad del Corpus Christi, Toledo, España
932: 
933: A passive daytime radiative cooling roof application can double the energy savings of a white roof, attributed to high solar reflectance and thermal emittance in the [infrared window](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infrared_window "Infrared window"),[\[118\]](#cite_note-:352-118) with the highest cooling potential in hot and dry cities such as [Phoenix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix,_Arizona "Phoenix, Arizona") and [Las Vegas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Las_Vegas "Las Vegas").[\[119\]](#cite_note-:36-119) When installed on roofs in dense urban areas, passive daytime radiative cooling panels can significantly lower outdoor surface temperatures at the pedestrian level.[\[10\]](#cite_note-:2-10)[\[11\]](#cite_note-:13-11)
934: 
935: ## Society and culture
936: 
937: \[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Urban_heat_island&action=edit&section=28 "Edit section: Society and culture")\]
938: 
939: ### History of research
940: 
941: \[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Urban_heat_island&action=edit&section=29 "Edit section: History of research")\]
942: 
943: The phenomenon was first investigated and described by [Luke Howard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luke_Howard_\(meteorologist\) "Luke Howard (meteorologist)") in the 1810s, although he was not the one to name the phenomenon.[\[120\]](#cite_note-120) A description of the very first report of the UHI by Luke Howard said that the urban center of London was warmer at night than the surrounding countryside by 2.1 °C (3.7 °F).[\[121\]](#cite_note-121)
944: 
945: Investigations of the urban atmosphere continued throughout the nineteenth century. Between the 1920s and the 1940s, researchers in the emerging field of local climatology or [microscale meteorology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microscale_meteorology "Microscale meteorology") in Europe, Mexico, India, Japan, and the United States pursued new methods to understand the phenomenon.
946: 
947: In 1929, Albert Peppler used the term in a German publication believed to be the first instance of an equivalent to urban heat island: *städtische Wärmeinsel* (which is *urban heat island* in German).[\[122\]](#cite_note-122) Between 1990 and 2000, about 30 studies were published annually; by 2010, that number had increased to 100, and by 2015, it was more than 300.[\[123\]](#cite_note-123)
948: 
949: Leonard O. Myrup published the first comprehensive numerical treatment to predict the effects of the urban heat island (UHI) in 1969.[\[33\]](#cite_note-:3-33) His paper surveys UHI and criticizes then-existing theories as being excessively qualitative.
950: 
951: ### Aspects of social inequality
952: 
953: \[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Urban_heat_island&action=edit&section=30 "Edit section: Aspects of social inequality")\]
954: 
955: **Urban heat inequity**, also termed thermal inequity, is an unequal distribution of heat in urban areas or neighborhoods within them, which causes disproportionate impacts to people living in those communities. Unequal threat of heat stress in urban environments is often correlated with differences in demographics, including racial and ethnic background, income, education level, and age.[\[49\]](#cite_note-:0-49) While the general impacts of urban heat inequity depend on the city studied, negative effects typically act on historically marginalized communities.[\[49\]](#cite_note-:0-49) The idea is closely tied to the urban heat island effect, where a major cause to urban heat inequity is increased urbanization.[\[48\]](#cite_note-:2a-48)
956: 
957: Some studies suggest that the effects of UHIs on health may be disproportionate, since the impacts may be unevenly distributed based on a variety of factors such as age,[\[69\]](#cite_note-WHO-69)[\[124\]](#cite_note-Diaz_article-124) ethnicity and socioeconomic status.[\[125\]](#cite_note-Harlan_article-125) This raises the possibility of health impacts from UHIs being an [environmental justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmental_justice "Environmental justice") issue. Studies have shown that [communities of color](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communities_of_color "Communities of color") in the United States have been disproportionately affected by UHI.[\[126\]](#cite_note-126)[\[127\]](#cite_note-127)[\[128\]](#cite_note-128)[\[129\]](#cite_note-Teron-129)
958: 
959: There is a correlation between neighborhood income and tree canopy cover.[\[130\]](#cite_note-Demand-130) Low-income neighborhoods tend to have significantly fewer trees than neighborhoods with higher incomes.[\[131\]](#cite_note-Income_Inequality-131) Researchers hypothesized that less-well-off neighborhoods do not have the financial resources to plant and maintain trees. [Affluent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affluent "Affluent") neighborhoods can afford more trees, on "both public and private property".[\[131\]](#cite_note-Income_Inequality-131) One reason for this discrepancy is that wealthier homeowners and communities can afford more land, which can be kept open as [green space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_belt "Green belt"), whereas poorer housing often takes the form of [rentals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renting "Renting"), where landowners try to maximize their [profit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Profit_\(economics\) "Profit (economics)") by putting as much housing [density](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population_density "Population density") as possible on their land.[\[132\]](#cite_note-132)
960: 
961: On a global scale, there are discrepancies in the effects of UHIs in different regions of the world. While overall heat exposure is increasing worldwide, its effects have increased faster in the Global South in recent decades, per a study by Professor Kanging Huang and colleagues.[\[133\]](#cite_note-133)
962: 
963: The disproportionate impact of UHIs on the Global South exacerbates already occurring environmental injustices. Because many countries in the equator are naturally hot and humid, these areas are particularly susceptible to the effects of UHIs. One World Bank study has found a 7.0° disparity between the hottest and coolest neighborhoods in Bandung, Indonesia.[\[134\]](#cite_note-134)
964: 
965: [![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4a/We_Parked_Our_Car_In_This_Worlds_Largest_Parking_Lot%2C_Between_16Th_And_26Th_Sts._On_Columbus_Drive_%28NBY_417663%29.jpg/250px-We_Parked_Our_Car_In_This_Worlds_Largest_Parking_Lot%2C_Between_16Th_And_26Th_Sts._On_Columbus_Drive_%28NBY_417663%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:We_Parked_Our_Car_In_This_Worlds_Largest_Parking_Lot,_Between_16Th_And_26Th_Sts._On_Columbus_Drive_\(NBY_417663\).jpg)
966:

### Urban design

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Urban_heat_island&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Urban design")\]

See also: [Urban design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_design "Urban design")

There are several causes of an urban heat island (UHI) related to common [urban design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_design "Urban design") aspects. For example, dark surfaces absorb significantly more [solar radiation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_radiation "Solar radiation"), which causes urban concentrations of roads and buildings to heat more than suburban and rural areas during the day;[\[2\]](#cite_note-dx.doi.org-2) materials commonly used in urban areas for pavement and roofs, such as [concrete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concrete "Concrete") and [asphalt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asphalt_concrete "Asphalt concrete"), have significantly different thermal bulk properties (including [heat capacity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Specific_heat_capacity "Specific heat capacity") and [thermal conductivity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermal_conductivity "Thermal conductivity")) and surface radiative properties ([albedo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albedo "Albedo") and [emissivity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emissivity "Emissivity")) than the surrounding rural areas. This causes a change in the [energy budget](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_energy_budget "Earth's energy budget") of the urban area, often leading to higher temperatures than surrounding rural areas.[\[35\]](#cite_note-Okeljnljn-35)
